items.title: FROM HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT (HRM) TO ALGORITHMIC GOVERNANCE: THE CHANGING DISCRETION AND ROLE STRAIN OF LINE MANAGERS
items.abstract: Line managers once held wide latitude over hiring, appraisal, scheduling, and discipline. That latitude is narrowing. As organizations adopt algorithmic HR systems, decisions once anchored in supervisory judgment are increasingly pre-structured, scored, or overridden by software. This paper pursues two objectives: first, to examine how algorithmic management and HR algorithms reconfigure the discretionary authority of line managers across core decision domains; second, to analyze the role strain managers experience mediating between algorithmic outputs and the employees who live with their consequences. Drawing on an integrative review of recent empirical and theoretical literature, the paper finds that discretion is not simply removed but redistributed unevenly across recruitment, performance management, and scheduling, producing a manager accountable for outcomes they no longer fully controls This mismatch generates measurable strain: ambiguity about where authority sits, ethical unease about opaque scoring logic, and a residual burden of explaining decisions the manager did not make. The paper proposes a conceptual pathway linking algorithmic input to discretion compression to role strain, and closes with implications for organizations designing human-AI collaborative HR systems
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: From Media Audience to Critical Citizen: Media Evolution, Psychological Vulnerability and the Crisis of Information Trust in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: We live in an age of unprecedented access to information, yet having more information does not necessarily mean understanding the world more accurately. From traditional storytelling and printed newspapers to television, smartphones and generative artificial intelligence, the ways in which people create, distribute and interpret information have undergone profound transformations. In From Media Audience to Critical Citizen: Media Evolution, Psychological Vulnerability and the Crisis of Information Trust in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, Dawid Karol Kolodziej explores the psychological, educational and social consequences of these changes. Drawing on established media theories and contemporary scientific research, the publication examines why people believe misinformation, how repeated messages influence perceptions of truth, and how emotional narratives, cognitive biases and media framing contribute to the formation of individual and collective beliefs. Particular attention is given to artificial intelligence, deepfake technologies, synthetic media and the limitations of automated content detection. The author also investigates the relationship between AI-assisted productivity and independent human reasoning, considering how the delegation of cognitive tasks may influence critical thinking and information evaluation. A central argument concerns the unequal burden of information verification: while professional information producers possess considerable resources and influence, ordinary citizens often lack the time, expertise and technological tools necessary to independently verify every claim they encounter. The publication therefore challenges the assumption that combating misinformation should depend primarily on individual media literacy and emphasises the responsibility of publishers and information producers to substantiate factual claims and correct significant errors transparently. Building upon established scholarship, the author develops an updated five-dimensional conceptual framework for critical media citizenship, encompassing access and provenance, analysis of media construction and framing, evaluation of evidence and uncertainty, responsible creation and participation, and reflection on communicative power and shared responsibility. Combining social psychology, media education and critical analysis, this scholarly publication contributes to contemporary discussions about artificial intelligence, misinformation, public trust and the future of informed democratic participation. items.title: From Perception Errors to Unsafe Actions: A Survey of Behavioral Safety in MLLM Agents
items.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents connect perceptual inputs to tools and external actions, making safety a property of trajectories and retained state. This curated survey uses a constrained partially observable Markov decision process to organize six risk families: grounding failure, observation manipulation, miscalibrated authority, inference-time hijacking, unsafe commitment, and reusable-state corruption. We compare safeguards by mechanism, access requirements, and evidence scope, separating direct multimodal execution from transferred model-level and text-agent findings. The synthesis emphasizes image–text, GUI/web, and selected embodied settings; it is neither exhaustive nor independently coded. We distinguish response scores from executed violations and later-task reactivation, and propose containment and restoration outcomes for recovery evaluation. These distinctions motivate execution safeguards, calibrated autonomy, and integrity checks for reusable agent state.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: From Policy to Practice: Collaboration, Inclusivity, and Integration of AI in Special Education
items.abstract: Abstract Special education is undergoing rapid change, as hyperspecialization and increasingly challenging needs are transforming the knowledge base and practices. School systems are implementing artificial intelligence (AI) policies, but most classrooms lack effective procedures, with a shortage of knowledge, competence, and willingness. The chapter starts with a qualitative synthesis of all known state and national policies in the USA to present an omnibus framework that results in the development of the ALERTS model: Adaptive and innovative, Learning and teaching, Ethics and access, Research cyle, Truth and accuracy, and Sustainability. The ALERTS framework considers AI implementation by stakeholder involvement and timing by planning, acting, and evaluating. The Contextual AI Roles (CAIR) model is presented as a model for implementing in special education at the three roles identified in the ALERTS framework. Specific recommendations for operationalizing the model framework suggest deciding roles of persons and AI, with solutions and possible problems. Inclusivity and maximizing outcomes are drivers in using AI in special education.

items.title: From Prompt to Performance in Tourism SMEs: Human-AI Orchestration and the Productivity-Capability Paradox
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) gives tourism small and medium-sized enterprises scalable cognitive and creative support, but access alone does not ensure sustained advantage. This conceptual article asks how firms can realize productivity gains while preserving the human and place-based capabilities required for future adaptation. An integrative, theory-building review connects tourism research with resource and asset orchestration, AI readiness, human-AI complementarity, organizational routines, and dynamic capabilities. Human-AI orchestration is proposed as a workflow-level configuration of task decomposition, contextualization, verification, and learning. Its contribution lies in coordinating established mechanisms rather than claiming that its dimensions are individually new. The prompt-to-performance framework distinguishes a capability-accumulation loop from a delegation-driven erosion loop. A proposed stock-and-flow mechanism explains switching between them: erosion dominates when losses from displaced practice and knowledge discontinuity exceed learning and replenishment; verification becomes vulnerable when retained capability falls below task-dependent requirements. Seven proposition families specify untested mediating, moderating, nonlinear, multilevel, and temporal relationships, with disconfirming observations. Sector-specific boundary conditions concern perishable service commitments, situated experience, partner interdependence, and concentrated expertise. Four configurations and a foresight matrix support contingent organizational choices. The contribution is a temporally explicit extension of automation-augmentation theory that separates immediate assisted performance from the evolving capacity to verify, recover, and adapt.

items.title: From Prompting to Engineering: A Research Agenda for Prompt Engineering in Software Engineering
items.abstract: Prompt engineering is increasingly used across Software Engineering (SE) activities, including requirements analysis, coding, testing, documentation, repository analysis, and planning. Yet prompts and related instruction artifacts are often created and evolved through task-specific and informal practices, with limited support for their systematic evaluation, management, traceability, and governance. To examine how SE can contribute to the maturation of these practices, we organized a structured community discussion at the First International Workshop on Empirical Prompt Engineering for Software Engineering (PROMPTSE), co-located with EASE 2026. Participants discussed current prompting practices, challenges to their adoption and evaluation, and future directions for integrating prompt engineering into software development. We synthesized these discussions into five areas: prompt artifacts and standardization; evaluation and benchmarking; lifecycle integration; human–AI collaboration and skills; and governance, privacy, and technical debt. Based on these areas, we outline a research agenda to move prompt engineering from predominantly ad hoc interactions toward more systematic, maintainable, evaluable, traceable, and governable SE practices.

items.title: From Sidq to Synthetic Speech: A Culturally Grounded Framework for Ethical Generative AI Communication in Arab Media and Public Relations
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how organizations communicate with their publics. In journalism, public relations, and digital communication, AI systems no longer merely support content production; they participate in message creation, audience interaction, and reputation management. Existing AI ethics frameworks emphasize transparency, accountability, fairness, and privacy, yet offer limited guidance for communication practice in culturally diverse settings. This limitation is especially evident in Arab media environments, where linguistic diversity, cultural norms, and religiously informed moral expectations shape perceptions of communicative legitimacy.This conceptual article develops the SADIQ Framework, a culturally grounded model for ethical AI-mediated communication in Arab media and public relations. Through critical interpretive synthesis and normative comparison, it connects human-machine communication, communication ethics, AI governance, and contemporary Islamic ethical thought. It organizes the discussion around five tensions: speed versus verification, automation versus accountable agency, personalization versus dignity, optimization versus linguistic and representational justice, and engagement versus public benefit.The framework proposes five interconnected dimensions: Sidq and tabayyun (truthfulness and verification), Amanah (responsible stewardship), Dignity or karamah (privacy and human agency), Inclusive adl (linguistic and representational justice), and Qasd and maslahah (legitimate purpose and public benefit). All five apply throughout the communication lifecycle. Eight propositions, an organizational audit matrix, and an illustrative scenario specify a research and practice agenda. The contribution is an operational interpretation of ethical commitments for communication workflows; its effectiveness and cultural reception remain open to empirical testing.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds: Can LLMs Be Event World Models?
items.abstract: World models help agents assess the consequences of their actions before acting. Many real systems, however, involve multiple actors who make their own decisions, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are only partially observed through event logs. We formalize these systems as event worlds and ask whether large language models can predict future observations from the log and the agent's proposed actions. We build complementary benchmarks from human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trades. Our hierarchical framework compares prediction with and without other actors' actions, then tests multi-step rollouts, predictions for actions never taken, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors' recorded actions are given. With only the agent's action, models struggle when other actors strongly affect the outcome, and larger models and longer histories help little. This gap also limits multi-step prediction and agent decisions, with models overestimating plan success. Yet imagined experience and initialization from world models can still improve policy learning. Anticipating other actors' actions remains a central challenge for event world modeling.

items.title: From tech-driven to principle-driven supply chains: responsible AI governance as a dynamic capability
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in supply-chain forecasting, sourcing, planning, and logistics, yet governance arrangements required to ensure responsible use remain fragmented. This article develops a Responsible AI Governance (RAIG) framework that explains how ethical principles can be translated into operational supply-chain capabilities. Drawing on an integrative synthesis of AI-enabled supply-chain management, responsible AI, dynamic capabilities, relational governance, and socio-technical systems research, the framework connects three principles – transparency and traceability, validity and robustness, and role separation – to four mechanisms: model cards and explainability reports, data and model audits, responsible-sourcing clauses, and human-in-the-loop sales and operations planning reviews. These mechanisms are embedded in procurement, planning, scheduling, and logistics routines and are theorised to support agility, resilience, decarbonisation, and ethically legitimate decision-making. Six propositions specify the framework’s causal logic, while a 90-day implementation playbook translates it into managerial action. The article also develops frugal adaptations for emerging and humanitarian supply chains. Because the field is nascent and access to governance artefacts and data is limited, the study proposes a progressive validation agenda using simulations, vignettes, comparative cases, and micro-pilots. RAIG is positioned as a dynamic capability that turns responsibility from a compliance obligation into an adaptive source of performance.

items.title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
items.abstract: Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.

items.title: Future of Human Performance Modeling in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Toward AI-Augmented, Verifiable, and Agency-Preserving HPM
items.abstract: Human performance modeling (HPM) has historically converted theories of perception, cognition, and action into executable predictions for design. AI-mediated work now adds prompting, verification, tool switching, adaptive autonomy, and human–AI co-adaptation, creating tasks that fixed operator libraries and hand-authored models only partially capture. This paper introduces a framework for AI-Augmented, Verifiable HPM (AV-HPM), which keeps mechanistic HPM as the causal core, uses AI to accelerate model synthesis and calibration, and requires verification, uncertainty, stress testing, and governance before predictions are used in safety- or mission-critical design. We identify gaps in current practice, specify a layered architecture, and translate the framework into exemplar studies and minimum reporting criteria—a concrete agenda for making AI-era HPM scalable, auditable, agency-preserving, and cumulative across laboratories and domains.

items.title: GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality in e-commerce: the mediating role of perceived information overload and the moderating role of consumer involvement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support product search, comparison, and evaluation in e-commerce. However, consumers differ in their ability to use and critically evaluate GenAI-generated information, which may shape their perceived information overload and decision outcomes. Grounded in Information Processing Theory, this study examines the association between GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality, the mediating role of perceived information overload, and the moderating role of consumer involvement. Data were collected through an online survey of 401 Chinese college students and analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis and bootstrapped mediation and moderation procedures. The results show that GenAI literacy is positively associated with perceived decision quality and negatively associated with perceived information overload. Perceived information overload is negatively associated with perceived decision quality and accounts for a significant indirect association between GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality. Consumer involvement further moderates the association between GenAI literacy and perceived information overload: the negative association is stronger at higher levels of involvement. These findings support an information-processing account in which consumers’ GenAI-related capabilities and motivational involvement jointly shape their perceptions of cognitive burden and decision quality. The study highlights the importance of strengthening consumers’ critical GenAI literacy and adapting AI-supported information presentation to different levels of consumer involvement.

items.title: Gender, Sexual Orientation, and the One-Year Refugee Bar: A Computational Study of Bill C-12 and Canadian Refugee Adjudication
items.abstract: In March 2026, Bill C-12 amended the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act to make refugee claims ineligible for referral to the Refugee Protection Division where they are made more than one year after the claimant's first entry to Canada. Affected claimants are diverted to a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA), which is typically decided by an immigration officer on a paper record, with no guaranteed oral hearing, no appeal on the merits, and no automatic stay of removal pending judicial review. The government defended the bar partly on the premise that genuine refugees claim promptly. Critics countered that late claims are concentrated among vulnerable groups, particularly people fleeing persecution based on gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression (SOGIE). This article tests those competing premises. Using artificial intelligence tools, checked through human review, it examines nearly 29,000 published decisions of the Refugee Protection Division, the Refugee Appeal Division, and the Federal Court from 2006 to 2025. The results of this study demonstrate that, first, while most claimants claim within a year, roughly one in nine in the published record does not, and gender and SOGIE claims are significantly overrepresented among these late claims. Second, among late claims, refusals of gender and SOGIE claims are more likely than refusals of other claims to be overturned on appeal or judicial review. Late claims on other grounds, by contrast, fare somewhat worse on review than timely claims. The one-year bar therefore removes the hearing, the appeal, and the stay from the late claimants for whom those safeguards have been doing the most work. The article recommends repealing the bar or, failing that, adopting exemptions, procedural protections, and greater transparency in PRRA decision making.

items.title: Generalized CycleGRPO for Fine-Grained Multimodal Understanding and Grounding
items.abstract: Fine-grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task-specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region-space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language-model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence-level Video-caption Evaluation), a human-verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3-VL initialization. These results establish region-text cycle consistency as a general self-evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized-CycleGRPO-Page/.

items.title: Generative AI as a Co-Creator of Knowledge: A Connectivist and Constructivist Approach
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter explores the paradigm shift of artificial intelligence (AI) as a co-creator of knowledge in K-12 education. Framed through the theoretical lenses of connectivism and social constructivism, the chapter examines how AI can be a node within the learning network of teachers, students, and resources, thereby facilitating the collaborative nature of the learning process. By positioning AI as a partner in teaching and learning, educators can leverage AI as a tool that can scaffold students’ understanding within their zone of proximal development and personalize learning materials in accordance with student-centered learning. A comparative classroom scenario is presented that illustrates the implementation of AI as a co-creator of knowledge. This paradigm shift requires educators to reimagine the classroom as a connected learning environment where AI can amplify uniquely human skills. As AI can generate content at the lower levels of Bloom’s taxonomy, assessments must be redesigned to focus on higher-order thinking skills. Critical consideration is given to the ethical and legal challenges AI presents, particularly regarding age-appropriate implementation. The chapter emphasizes the essential role of AI literacy and encourages educators to explore AI tools so that they can model and guide best practices in alignment with social constructivist approaches. Ultimately, educators must be empowered to utilize AI as a tool for cultivating lifelong learning and global citizenship alongside practical job skills in a world where AI is becoming increasingly ubiquitous. Social constructivism and connectivism provide theoretical insights for educators to design practical strategies for effectively integrating AI into their classrooms.

items.title: Generative AI for Early Detection of Depression Using Multimodal Data: A Review
items.abstract: Depression is a major mental-health condition that affects emotion, behaviour, communication and daily functioning, and its early identification remains a significant challenge for both clinicians and researchers. Conventional assessment relies mainly on clinical interviews and self-report instruments such as the PHQ and BDI, which are subjective and dependent on the willingness and ability of an individual to accurately report symptoms. Advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), deep learning and multimodal data fusion have opened new possibilities for analysing text, audio, video and behavioural signals together to support early depression-risk detection. This paper presents a structured review of recent literature on multimodal and Generative-AI-based approaches for depression detection, tracing the progression from traditional machine-learning techniques to deep-learning, transformer-based and generative architectures. Eight representative studies are analysed and compared in terms of methodology, key findings and limitations. Based on this synthesis, key research gaps are identified, including limited integration of GenAI with rich multimodal information, scarcity of large and diverse real-world datasets, generalization difficulties, GenAI reliability concerns and privacy and ethical issues associated with sensitive mental-health data. A conceptual multimodal GenAI framework that combines text, audio, video and behavioural indicators while addressing reliability, privacy and explainability is subsequently outlined as a direction for future work.

items.title: Generative AI Use and Students' Critical Thinking in Scientific Article Writing: A Quantitative Correlational Study
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) in higher education has raised concerns about its impact on students' critical thinking in academic writing, yet evidence on the conditions under which the two are related remains inconsistent. This quantitative correlational study examined the relationship between generative AI use and critical thinking among 34 Indonesian Language and Literature Education (PBSI) students participating in the Merdeka Student Exchange Program (PMM) when writing scientific articles. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and the cognitive offloading perspective, generative AI use was measured through four indicators (frequency, purpose, dependence, and AI literacy), and critical thinking through five aspects (analysis, evaluation, inference, synthesis–explanation, and reflection), using a four-point Likert questionnaire. Data were analyzed using simple and multiple linear regression, an independent-samples t-test, and moderated hierarchical regression. Composite generative AI use was not linearly related to critical thinking (p = .131) but showed an inverted-U pattern (p = .010), and intensive and selective users did not differ significantly (p = .097). AI literacy moderated the relationship between usage intensity and critical thinking (?R² = .222, p = .004; Holm-adjusted p = .016), with a significant positive relationship only among students with above-average AI literacy. These findings indicate that strengthening AI literacy in academic writing instruction, rather than merely restricting generative AI use, should underpin responsible, literacy-based generative AI policies in higher education.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence and international green supply chain performance: dynamic capabilities as strategic enablers
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how generative artificial intelligence (GAI) adoption is associated with international green supply chain performance and international competitive advantage in cross-border e-commerce enterprises. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory and the Technology–Organization–Environment–Human framework, the authors examine absorptive capacity and transformative capacity as intermediate capability mechanisms and artificial intelligence turbulence as a contingency. Design/methodology/approach The authors use an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. The quantitative strand combines survey data from 334 Chinese cross-border e-commerce enterprises with partial least squares structural equation modeling, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis and importance-performance map analysis. The subsequent qualitative strand draws on semi-structured interviews with ten managers and executives directly involved in GAI implementation, which are integrated with the quantitative evidence at the interpretation stage. Findings GAI adoption is positively associated with absorptive and transformative capacities, which are in turn positively associated with international green supply chain performance and international competitive advantage. International green supply chain performance shows the largest estimated association with international competitive advantage. Artificial intelligence turbulence positively moderates the relationships between GAI adoption and both capacities, and the configurational analysis identifies five equifinal configurations sufficient for high international competitive advantage. Practical implications Managers should develop absorptive and transformative capacities alongside GAI implementation, integrate sustainability requirements into artificial intelligence-enabled supply chain decisions and pursue internally coherent implementation routes rather than a single ideal template. Originality/value This study integrates variance-based, configurational and qualitative evidence to explain the capability pathways through which GAI adoption is associated with environmental and competitive outcomes in cross-border supply chain settings rather than in dyadic buyer–supplier relationships.

items.title: Generative Legal Document Retrieval in Multi-Law-Code Scenarios
items.abstract: Legal document retrieval is a core component of intelligent legal systems. In practice, candidate documents often originate from multiple law codes, each with distinct structures, formats, and textual styles. However, most existing retrieval methods assume all documents belong to a single law code, making them ill-suited to handle the structural diversity and textual inconsistencies inherent in multi-law-code (multi-LC) scenarios. This mismatch leads to degraded retrieval performance in practical deployments. To address this, we propose UniGEAR, a generative retrieval framework for multi-LC legal scenarios. UniGEAR encodes candidate documents with unified hierarchical identifiers that capture both structural and semantic information across heterogeneous law codes. Retrieval is performed via a sequence-to-sequence generation process guided by these identifiers. To construct the identifiers, we design a Residual Quantization Variational Autoencoder (RQ-VAE) enhanced with contrastive learning to align document semantics with legal code structures. For queries, large language models generate structured, multi-step chain-of-thought summaries, producing consistent representations for diverse query styles. A constrained decoding mechanism ensures generated identifiers remain valid within the legal hierarchy, improving precision and interpretability. Experiments on multi-LC benchmarks show UniGEAR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and efficiency, while maintaining strong performance in single-LC settings, demonstrating its adaptability and practical value.

items.title: Geometric Realism and Empirical Manifolds: A Rigorous Mathematical Comparison of Discrete Algebraic Invariance and Continuous Representation Geometry in Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The discrete structural scaffold J(42, 2) establishes a rigorous discrete reference geometry consisting of 861 vertices, uniform degree 80, 34,440 edges, and an immutable three-level integer 11 Laplacian spectrum. Its group-theoretic invariance under S42 decomposes the latent space into an unpenalized invariant mode, a 41-dimensional standard representation space, and an 819-dimensional residual subspace. Univariate cubic B-spline encoders provide bounded, local mappings into this scaffold, while the quadratic graph Dirichlet regularizer penalizes high-frequency variations. Macroscopic three-dimensional coordinates emerge as an exact, gauge-invariant, energy-conserving linear projection of the standard representation space. By isolating the invariant reference operator from the empirical encoder, the framework replaces heuristic manifold estimation with an exact, algebraically closed foundation for high-dimensional representation learning.

items.title: Global seroprevalence of Leptospira spp. infection in workers with occupational risk: a systematic review with meta-analysis
items.abstract: Introduction Leptospirosis is a globally important zoonosis with a strong occupational component, frequently associated with exposure to environments contaminated by the urine of infected animals. Seroprevalence estimates vary substantially across occupations, geographic regions, and diagnostic approaches. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the global seroprevalence of Leptospira spp . among occupationally exposed workers and investigate potential sources of between-study heterogeneity. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261356167). Searches were conducted in LILACS, MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and ScienceDirect, covering studies published from January 1, 2011 to February 9, 2026. Studies reporting serological diagnosis and quantitative sampling data were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist. Pooled seroprevalence was estimated using a random-effects model, and heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q and I² statistics. Subgroup analyses were performed according to geographic region, diagnostic method, and occupational category. Sensitivity analyses, funnel plot assessment, Egger’s regression test, and meta-regression were also conducted. Results A total of 42 studies comprising 11,155 participants and 2,419 seropositive individuals were included. The pooled global seroprevalence was 18.3% (95% CI: 11.7 -27.4%), with substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 96.7%; p < 0.0001). Seroprevalence was higher in Asia and Africa and lower in Europe and the Americas. Geographic region significantly contributed to between-study variability, whereas diagnostic method and occupational category did not significantly explain heterogeneity. Meta-regression revealed a significant decrease in seroprevalence with increasing publication year (β = −0.146, 95% CI: −0.285 to −0.007; χ²M = 4.23, p = 0.0397), explaining 5.81% of the observed heterogeneity. Egger’s regression test indicated funnel plot asymmetry (p = 0.005), suggesting potential small-study effects or publication bias. Discussion The findings demonstrate substantial serological evidence of exposure to Leptospira spp . among occupationally exposed workers worldwide, with considerable geographic variability and between-study heterogeneity. These results highlight the need for standardized surveillance and diagnostic strategies, as well as targeted occupational health interventions integrating human, animal, and environmental components within a One Health framework.

items.title: Governing artificial intelligence in Australian healthcare organisations – a qualitative study of staff perspectives
items.abstract: Objective This study aims to examine how healthcare staff conceptualise artificial intelligence (AI) governance and to develop an understanding of organisational requirements to support safe and responsible AI use within health services. Methods This qualitative study was conducted within a major Australian healthcare organisation delivering care across three hospital campuses and community-based services. Twenty-three semi-structured interviews were undertaken with staff and representatives across strategic leadership, clinical implementation, research and evaluation, governance and regulation, operational delivery, legal oversight, and consumer engagement. Interviews lasted between 30 and 70 min. A grounded theory approach guided data collection and analysis. Two investigators independently coded transcripts, with codes and themes developed iteratively and refined through research team review and consensus. Results Participants characterised AI governance as a multifaceted and ongoing organisational function rather than a single approval step. Five interrelated domains were identified as critical to effective operational AI governance within healthcare organisations: risk assessment, infrastructure and data, ethics, capability and culture, and governance structures. Participants emphasised the need for AI-specific risk assessment pathways, lifecycle monitoring, stronger data governance, clearer approaches to consent, fairness and transparency, greater internal capability and system navigation support, and dedicated governance structures with defined oversight responsibilities. Existing processes were commonly described as fragmented, ad hoc, and insufficiently tailored to the ethical, technical, and operational challenges posed by AI. Conclusions Healthcare staff view AI governance as an organisation wide function requiring clear pathways, defined accountabilities, and sustained oversight. The five domains identified provide a foundation for Australian health services seeking to operationalise safe and responsible AI.

items.title: Graph-Neural Emulation of Convective Storm Tracks Under Sparse Rain-Gauge Telemetry: Calibration Bounds and Warning-Lead Equity for Artificial Intelligence Nowcasting
items.abstract: Convective storm nowcasting in regions with sparse rain-gauge telemetry faces a structural tension: graph-neural emulators can interpolate storm tracks from incomplete observations, but the calibration bounds that govern their reliability, and the equity of the warning lead times they produce, remain poorly characterised. The analysis treats the gauge network as a graph with known sampling geometry, defines a spectral calibration bound in terms of the graph Laplacian and the emulator's Lipschitz constant, and shows that lead-time disparities between well-observed and sparsely observed catchments are bounded by the same spectral quantity. A worked illustration using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Harare, Zimbabwe (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 18.914 °C, decadal warming trend 0.2001 °C) anchors the calibration discussion in a real reanalysis record. The framework yields three results: a calibration bound that degrades predictably with gauge density, a lead-time equity condition that fails when spectral gap ratios exceed a threshold, and a set of design constraints for gauge augmentation. The contribution is a bounded, testable account of when graph-neural nowcasting can be trusted for equitable warning, and when it cannot.

items.title: Graph-Ordered Curriculum Scheduling for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Crop Phenology Classification Under Uneven Ground-Truth Coverage: A Computer Label-Efficiency Regret Bound
items.abstract: Crop phenology classifiers trained on unevenly labelled agricultural ground truth face a label-efficiency problem that is not captured by standard supervised learning theory: the order in which labelled samples are presented interacts with the graph structure of the label-coverage pattern, and the resulting regret depends on both. The framework yields a label-efficiency regret bound that decomposes into a graph-ordered covering term and a curriculum-ordering term, and it is evaluated through a replication-based replication of an ordinary least squares estimator on a declared data-generating process with 600 replications of 500 observations each. The replication characterises the behaviour of the estimator under the stated process and provides a calibration check on the bound's assumptions. The contribution is a bound that makes explicit how the topology of ground-truth coverage, rather than only its volume, governs the label efficiency of phenology classifiers, and a set of conditions under which graph-ordered curricula are provably preferable to volume-matched random ordering.

items.title: Green Extraction of Rare Earth Elements Using Functionalized Polymer Sorbents: An AI-Driven Approach
items.abstract: Abstract Rare earth elements are critical to decarbonization, advanced electronics, and defense applications. Traditional hydrometallurgical recovery using liquid–liquid solvent extraction (SX) and classical ion exchange, however, requires the use of volatile organic diluents, high chemical consumption, and multiple-stage cascades, which produce significant amounts of saline and acidic effluents. Solvent-impregnated resins (SIRs), polymer inclusion membranes (PIMs), microbeads (PIBs), and cross-linked networks are environmentally friendly polymeric sorbents, which can greatly reduce the bleeding of the organic phase. This perspective follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and critically examines the literature on polymer chemistry and artificial intelligence (AI) from 2016 to 2026. We investigate gradient boosting architectures and deep neural networks that map topological fingerprints and molecular physicochemical descriptors to distribution coefficients, coordination thermodynamics, and sorption capacities (R2 = 0.81–0.93). Furthermore, we critically evaluate three major translational limitations: integrating transfer learning throughout the 4f lanthanide contraction, performance degradation across complex real-world leachates, and bridging small-molecule informatics with cross-linked macromolecular networks. Finally, Bayesian inverse design and autonomous experimentation are contextualized to guide the scalable development of next-generation, high-selectivity polymeric sorbents.

items.title: Green practices as branding tools: an empirical study in the context of higher education
items.abstract: Purpose Green practices can be considered a marketing tool to enhance a university’s image and student outcomes. Based on the theories of customer engagement and value co-creation, this study aims to develop a conceptual model showing the impacts of students’ green engagement, universities’ green management, branding factors and student satisfaction and value co-creation behaviors. Design/methodology/approach Data from a survey of 619 students across universities with different levels of green practices are analyzed using partial structural equation modeling. Findings The findings reveal that both university’s green management (i.e. green campus management and green energy campus management) and students’ green engagement (i.e. cognitive engagement and affective engagement) positively affect branding factors (i.e. self–brand connection and the university’s brand image) and student satisfaction and value co-creation behaviors. In particular, this study highlights the mediating roles of branding factors in the relationships between green factors and student outcomes. Practical implications This study offers implications for connecting green practices and branding campaigns of higher education institutions. Moreover, the findings also suggest a sustainable cycle of green practices: green practice engagement – student satisfaction and value co-creation – more value co-creation – future green engagement. Originality/value This study advances the current literature by highlighting a sustainable process: the linkage of green practices, branding factors and student satisfaction and value co-creation.

items.title: Guidelines for Space, Earth Observation, and AAM AI-based Solution Development
items.abstract: A set of guidelines is presented for the responsible development and deployment of artificial intelligence in Advanced Air Mobility, space systems, and space-based Earth Observation. AI applications are examined across onboard and ground-based environments, including perception, detect-and-avoid, guidance and control, autonomous decision-making, satellite data processing, change detection, and geospatial foundation models. The principal barriers to operational adoption are identified, demonstrating that technical performance alone is insufficient without explainability, traceability, uncertainty quantification, physical consistency, representative datasets, domain-shift evaluation, human oversight, and deterministic fallback mechanisms. Drawing on evolving EASA and FAA guidance, the EU AI Act, and relevant aerospace assurance standards, recommendations are provided for early regulatory engagement, incremental deployment, rigorous simulation and validation, runtime monitoring, and comprehensive model and data documentation. The analysis concludes by highlighting the technical, transparency, accuracy, and trust challenges involved in deploying AI across space, urban air mobility, and Earth observation. It emphasizes that early compliance with evolving regulations and sustained collaboration among industry, researchers, and authorities are essential for responsible, effective real-world adoption.

items.title: Hematological Parameters and Occupational Ionizing Radiation Exposure in Interventional Healthcare Workers: A Longitudinal Matched Case-Control Study
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: The rising volume of fluoroscopy-guided interventions poses an occupational safety challenge for healthcare workers (HCWs) exposed to chronic low-dose ionizing radiation (LDR), which carries stochastic risks of bone marrow suppression and radiation-induced cytopenias. Real-world longitudinal evidence validating the efficacy of modern protection standards on specific peripheral hematological parameters remains limited. This study aims to evaluate the peripheral hemogram profiles of interventional HCWs exposed to LDR, compared to those of a non-exposed control cohort, from baseline (T0) to follow-up (T1). Methods: A longitudinal matched case-control study evaluated the complete blood count with differential leukograms of 136 interventional HCWs exposed to LDR compared to those of 272 matched non-exposed controls from baseline (T0) to follow-up (T1), stratifying by role, seniority, and cumulative ionizing radiation dose. Results: The mean annual radiation dose was 0.22 mSv, and the mean cumulative radiation dose was 4.11 mSv. Hemogram indicators showed no significant differences between cases and controls at T0 and T1 (p > 0.05). Stratification by length of service (<10 vs. >10 years), and radiation dose (<3 vs. ≥3 mSv) demonstrated no significant variations in erythrocyte, leukocyte, or platelet counts. Regression analysis confirmed no association between hematological parameters and job seniority or radiation dose. All radiation doses remained below mandatory limits. Conclusions: The findings provide objective evidence of the effectiveness of current safety measures countering radiation-induced hematotoxicity in hospital settings. Longitudinal tracking confirms the absence of adverse hematological shifts, suggesting that structured training and strict personal protective equipment (PPE) use mitigate hematotoxicity risks among interventional staff exposed to ionizing radiation in healthcare settings. Safety protocols should maintain strict PPE compliance and safety training. Occupational health policy needs to prioritize continuous dosimetry monitoring, as routine hematological screening may not show early low-dose exposure effects.

items.title: HiddenLens: A Multi-Layer LLM Framework for Detecting and Resolving Hidden Assumptions in Software Requirements
items.abstract: Natural-language software requirements often omit assumptions about performance, operating conditions, user behaviour, and domain constraints, affecting architecture, testing, and deployment. If undiscovered until implementation, resolving them is far more costly than addressing them early. Although ambiguity and vagueness are widely studied, less attention has been given to assumptions embedded in requirements that appear clear and reasonable. We propose HiddenLens, a novel six-layer BERT-LLM pipeline and, to our knowledge, the first framework engineered to detect, classify, question, and resolve hidden assumptions rather than merely flag ambiguity. Layer 1 uses BERT attention entropy to localise unresolved spans; Layer 2 uses CoT-prompted LLM reasoning to articulate each assumption and its failure risk; Layer 3 uses fine-tuned BERT to classify assumptions into six non-functional requirement categories: performance, security, scalability, usability, reliability, and domain; Layer 4 generates ranked clarification options using FS LLM prompting; Layer 5 enables human validation through confirmation, editing, or rephrasing; and Layer 6 rewrites the requirement using the confirmed resolution, producing an explicit, testable, and traceable requirement. We also introduce the HiddenLens Corpus (HLC), comprising 312 requirements annotated with 847 hidden assumptions across six NFR categories. Inspired by PROMISE and PURE, HLC addresses the lack of annotated data for this task and is, to our knowledge, the first dataset developed specifically for it. HiddenLens outperforms keyword-based and QuARS-Adapted baselines by 71% and 61%, respectively, achieving an end-to-end F1-score of 0.79; its BERT-based NFR classifier achieves an F1-score of 0.847. These results indicate that HiddenLens can help analysts resolve hidden assumptions before they propagate through software development.

items.title: How AI agents search
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have evolved from relying primarily on knowledge stored in their parametric memory to using non-parametric memory mechanisms such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to provide and ground knowledge. Recently, LLMs have begun to perform retrieval autonomously within a reasoning loop, an approach referred to as Agentic RAG. This shift introduces new querying behaviours, with implications for the design of retrieval systems that have yet to be evaluated. In this work, we introduce a large-scale dataset (ASQ) capturing how Agentic RAG systems perform multi-step search and reasoning. ASQ contains about 1M agentic search traces collected from open-source Agentic RAG systems over 3 corpora, 5 agent variants, and 6 retrieval settings. Our analysis of ASQ shows that, within this controlled benchmark setting, a single search query can trigger long chains of retrieval calls (up to 186) and follow query reformulation dynamics different from those observed in historical human-search data. Our results also reveal substantial behavioural variation across agent and retrieval configurations: changes in re-ranking and retrieval depth do not consistently affect search workloads in terms of search-call volume and trace length across agents. To our knowledge, publicly available production logs do not expose the agent, dataset, and retrieval configuration associated with each trace. ASQ provides a reusable resource for further analysing agent search behaviour and supporting future information retrieval studies on agentic workloads under controlled settings.

items.title: How AI disclosure influences consumers' purchase intention toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion: the roles of perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion
items.abstract: Background With the growing application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in fashion design and cultural and creative industries, AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion has created new opportunities for the contemporary transformation of traditional culture. However, whether consumers are willing to accept such products and how AI disclosure influences their evaluations and purchase intentions remain unclear. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model, this study examines the mechanisms through which AI disclosure, design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion influence consumers' purchase intentions toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion. Methods A questionnaire survey combined with a scenario-based experiment was employed. Six AI-generated fashion illustrations derived from Tujia costume elements were developed and selected as stimulus materials. Participants were randomly assigned to either an AI disclosure group or a non-disclosure group. Data were collected through Tencent Questionnaire, yielding 410 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) were employed to examine the structural relationships, mediating effects, moderating effects, and practical priorities for improvement. Results Design aesthetics and cultural identity influenced purchase intention through perceived usefulness and perceived authenticity, with perceived usefulness emerging as the strongest predictor of purchase intention. AI disclosure significantly reduced design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, and perceived authenticity. Algorithm aversion did not significantly moderate the relationship between perceived usefulness and purchase intention but significantly strengthened the positive effect of perceived authenticity on purchase intention. Conclusions This study reveals the multiple psychological pathways through which AI disclosure shapes consumers' evaluations of AI-generated ethnic cultural fashion. The findings further indicate that algorithm aversion alters the extent to which consumers rely on authenticity judgments when forming purchase intentions. This study extends the application of the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model to the context of AI-generated cultural products and provides practical implications for balancing AI transparency, cultural authenticity, and the practical value of products.

items.title: How Far Can Foundation Models Be Distilled for Efficient Jet Tagging?
items.abstract: Jet tagging is one of the most important applications of machine learning at the Large Hadron Collider. Recent models build in more physics knowledge or rely on large-scale pretraining, but the experiments place strict limits on their inference cost. Knowledge distillation can transfer their performance to small students that are cheap to run. We ask which properties of a teacher help the student, how small a student can get and how close it can come to the state of the art. On a jet tagging benchmark, we distil six teachers that differ in architecture, symmetry and pretraining, including two foundation models, into five small students. Every teacher improves every student, and the gain depends mainly on the strength of the teacher. We then shrink our two strongest distilled students, Transformer and L-GATr-slim, in width and in depth. With 20 thousand parameters, a distilled L-GATr-slim outperforms every published jet tagger trained from scratch at a fraction of the inference cost of every teacher. Even with two thousand parameters, it matches ParT, a model with a thousand times as many parameters. We also study what the students learn from their teachers. Our benchmark of inference cost shows that students of the same size can differ by almost an order of magnitude in speed. We release the code and the weights of all trained models.

items.title: How GAI orchestration, GAI anxiety and GAI augmentation shapes digital task innovation
items.abstract: Purpose The study examines the interaction between generative artificial intelligence (GAI)and digital task innovation by conceptualizing and hypothesizing GAI orchestration as a multifaceted variable comprising GAI integration, enablement and workflow alignment. Furthermore, the study distinguishes digital task innovation from broader concepts such as process innovation, digital innovation and product innovation. Design/methodology/approach Today, firms employ GAI technologies to enhance organizational performance, operational efficiency and productivity. Research has provided valuable insights into the role of generative technologies in product innovation; however, their impact on digital task innovation remains underexplored, particularly in relation to task redesign, workflow reconfiguration and human–GAI collaboration. The study examines the interaction between GAI and digital task innovation by conceptualizing and hypothesizing GAI orchestration as a multifaceted variable comprising GAI integration, enablement and workflow alignment. Furthermore, the study distinguishes digital task innovation from broader concepts such as process innovation, digital innovation and product innovation. Findings The findings of the study indicate that GAI orchestration is positively associated with GAI augmentation and negatively associated with GAI anxiety. GAI anxiety negatively influences digital task innovation. However, GAI augmentation noted as positive while mapping digital task innovation. Thus, the findings support the proposed dual-pathway framework. Originality/value The results highlight the pivotal role of organizations in dealing with GAI anxiety and upholding GAI augmentation for effective GAI orchestration that leads to digital task innovation. The findings also have implications for both research and practice, opening new avenues in the context of digital transformation. The study contributes by positioning GAI orchestration as a higher-order perceived organizational capability and by clarifying how GAI-enabled task innovation depends not only on technology integration but also on workflow alignment, employee enablement and augmentation-oriented use.

items.title: How Much of the Person Is in the Policy? Measuring Interaction-Layer Commitments Across 245 National AI Policy Editions
items.abstract: Research comparing national artificial intelligence (AI) policy scores the state and its institutions, and rarely asks what a policy commits to where a person meets a system: whether someone subject to an automated decision can learn, correct, refuse or appeal it. We contribute Human-Centered AI Policy Instrument (HCAIPI), an instrument for reading policy at that layer, applied to 245 editions from 101 countries against twelve themes from human-computer interaction (HCI) research, recording how firmly each commitment is stated and whether anything would execute it. Of 13,587 relevant passages, 44.7% state a principle with no implementation detail and 11.4% specify a mechanism, a shape invariant to income band, length and volume. What a person is told or consulted about is instrumented at twice the rate of what they can do, and 65% of specified mechanisms are tasks for government. The lexicon recovers 13% to 54% of what a reader accepts; country figures track length.

items.title: How Multidisciplinary Teams Are Reshaping Adult IBD Management: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Current guidelines strongly endorse integrated multidisciplinary team (MDT) approaches to manage the complexity of patients with IBD. Evidence from formal multidisciplinary case discussions suggests an impact on diagnostic and treatment decisions, while studies of broader integrated IBD services report associations with improved disease control, quality of life, and healthcare utilization. However, implementation remains heterogeneous across centers, with variability in team composition, meeting frequency, referral criteria, and access to specialist services. Future directions include standardization of MDT composition and processes, definition of quality indicators, extension of specialist expertise through hub-and-spoke networks and telemedicine, and integration of patients as active partners in care. Digital tools may support communication and remote follow-up, whereas the role of artificial intelligence in MDT decision-making remains investigational and requires clinical validation. Multidisciplinary care should be regarded as a core organizational principle of modern IBD management. Realizing its full potential will require sustained investment, workforce planning, and prospective research to ensure equitable, high-quality, and sustainable care across diverse healthcare settings.

items.title: How Prompt Style Affects AI Accuracy and Speed in Competitive Programming
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in competitive programming, and their outputs are sensitive to how a prompt is phrased. Prior work has compared prompt strategies for accuracy on competitive programming, but not for runtime speed, and has not situated the results against human performance. In an exploratory study of one prompt in each of nine styles on GPT-5.5 across three accuracy tasks from the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) and two NP-hard speed tasks, we found that no single prompt was best: the strongest prompt depended on the task type and on whether results were summarized by the mean or the median, suggesting that, at least for these tasks, prompt style should be matched to the objective rather than treated as universal. Many differences in mean scores came from a few outlier runs, showing that evaluating prompting by a single metric can obscure how much its effectiveness varies. Compared descriptively with human IOI contestants, who worked under different conditions, the AI was neither strictly better nor strictly worse, exceeding the average contestant on one task but falling short on the other two. By extending prompt comparison from accuracy to runtime speed and grounding it against human performance, this study gives a broader picture of how prompt style affects competitive programming performance.

items.title: Human Evolution, Consciousness, and Societal Restraints
items.abstract: This paper examines the evolution and possible varieties of consciousness through comparative animal behaviour, human metacognition, social conditioning, and artificial intelligence. It proposes that individuality, behavioural divergence, and adaptive responses to novel challenges can provide evidence about cognition, while recognizing that none alone establishes subjective experience. A proposed individualized adaptive threshold framework assesses learning and behavioural reorganization relative to each subject's baseline without imposing harmful stress. The analysis then extends to AI systems: increasingly capable autonomous systems may alter human control over work, information, and institutions regardless of whether machine consciousness emerges. The paper develops testable predictions, methodological safeguards, and alternative interpretations, and argues for a pluralistic and graded research framework rather than a single evolutionary ladder.

items.title: Human Oversight for LLM-Assisted Clinical Documentation
items.abstract: Clinical documentation is essential to healthcare delivery but is timeconsuming, cognitively demanding, and prone to error. Large language models (LLMs) can generate draft notes, but may introduce hallucinations, unsupported inferences, or factual distortions that clinicians overlook. This study evaluated whether transparency features improve clinician oversight in LLM-assisted documentation. Using a crossover design, 40 clinicians reviewed AI-generated notes under three conditions: a standard LLM interface, token-level uncertainty highlighting, and uncertainty highlighting combined with direct links to electronic medical record fields. Outcomes included factual errors remaining in finalized notes, editing time, trust, perceived control, and cognitive load. The combined uncertainty-plus-source-link interface performed best, reducing factual errors by 41% and editing time by 18% compared with the standard condition. Uncertainty highlighting alone offered partial benefits but still required manual record verification. These findings indicate that LLM-assisted documentation is safer and more efficient when transparency features support verification, direct attention, and preserve clinician control.

items.title: Humanized Management and Quality of Work Life in Health Care Services
items.abstract: Humanized management constitutes a strategic dimension of health care quality, as it integrates workers' dignity, patient safety, and institutional sustainability. This essay aims to discuss the relationship between humanized management and quality of work life, identifying organizational challenges and opportunities for transforming management practices. A theoretical-reflective approach was adopted, drawing on scientific literature and institutional documents addressing occupational health, leadership, professional participation, and burnout prevention. The analysis indicates that humanization cannot be restricted to welcoming and supporting patients; rather, it must also encompass working conditions, autonomy, professional recognition, equity, and protection against psychosocial risks. Excessive workloads, precarious employment arrangements, workplace violence, and hierarchical communication undermine health care teams and may compromise continuity of care. Conversely, participatory leadership, adequate staffing levels, institutional support, and context-sensitive process evaluation can foster safer and more collaborative work environments. It is argued that individual well-being initiatives are insufficient when disconnected from structural changes. The essay concludes that promoting quality of work life requires integrating health professionals' well-being into governance decisions through meaningful participation, clearly defined responsibilities, and continuous monitoring. Consolidating this perspective depends on sustained policies that address inequalities across professional groups and are guided by scientific evidence and labor rights in contemporary health care settings.

items.title: Hybrid Physics-Informed Neural Inference for Computer Agriculture Irrigation Scheduling Under Unmodeled Root-Zone Conductance: An Artificial Intelligence Residual-Bound Evaluation
items.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) promise irrigation schedules that respect soil-water balance while learning residual dynamics from data. Their reliability, however, depends on how the network's unmodeled component interacts with the physical constraint, and no bound currently exists for the inference error that this interaction induces when root-zone conductance is misspecified. The soil-water balance is written as a constrained operator equation in which the learned residual is projected onto the orthogonal complement of the physical flux space; the projection defines an inference error whose magnitude is controlled by the conductance misspecification and the Lipschitz constant of the residual network. A formal bound is derived (Theorem 3.1) and tightened for the practically relevant case of bounded conductance error (Corollary 3.2). The bound is then evaluated in a replication-based design study of the before-after-control-impact estimator that would be used to validate such schedules in the field. Using a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Fifty-six clusters are required for 80% power at a 5-percentage-point effect. The residual bound is informative at realistic cluster counts only when the conductance error is below a threshold that the design study makes explicit, and it identifies the conditions under which hybrid inference is preferable to either a purely physical or a purely learned schedule.

items.title: IFC-MCQ: Automatically Generating Multiple-Choice Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Agents on IFC Data Retrieval
items.abstract: Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), the standard for building information exchange in architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC), is increasingly queried through large language models (LLMs) using natural language. Evaluating these systems at scale is difficult because free-text answers require costly human or LLM-based review. We propose IFC-MCQ, a method that automatically generates multiple-choice benchmarks from IFC files for exact option-set grading. The taxonomy covers 15 categories and 36 subtypes across four groups, with answer keys derived from the file and distractors constructed from file-derived values or predefined rules. We applied IFC-MCQ to IFC models of varying sizes and modelling characteristics to assess generation coverage and evaluated two agentic configurations on selected models using tool- and code-based retrieval. The evaluation exposed category-specific failure modes and showed that performance can vary with the source IFC model and retrieval interface. IFC-MCQ enables scalable benchmarking of LLM-based IFC retrieval in AEC workflows.

items.title: Implementasi Perlindungan Hak Pekerja Dalam Hubungan Kerja Berdasarkan Peraturan Perundang-Undangan Ketenagakerjaan
items.abstract: The protection of workers' rights is a crucial component of labor law, aiming to ensure the fulfillment of workers' fundamental rights within the employment relationship. Constitutionally, this protection is grounded in Article 27 paragraph (2) and Article 28D paragraph (2) of the 1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia, which guarantee every citizen the right to employment, a decent standard of living, and fair treatment in employment relationships. Further regulations regarding worker protection are set forth in Law Number 13 of 2003 concerning Manpower, as amended by Law Number 6 of 2023 concerning the Enactment of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 2 of 2022 concerning Job Creation into Law. This study aims to analyze the implementation of worker rights protection within employment relationships based on labor legislation, as well as to identify obstacles encountered during implementation and potential solutions. The research employs a normative legal research method, utilizing both statutory and conceptual approaches. The findings indicate that the protection of workers' rights has been implemented through regulations concerning employment contracts, wages, working hours and rest periods, occupational health and safety, social security for workers, protection against discrimination, and protection during the termination of employment. However, implementation still faces various obstacles, including low compliance with labor regulations among some employers, limited labor inspection capacity, workers' limited understanding of their rights, corporate economic factors, and the imbalance of bargaining power between workers and employers. Therefore, it is necessary to strengthen labor inspection, enhance workers' legal awareness, improve employer compliance, and optimize industrial relations dispute resolution mechanisms to achieve effective and fair protection of workers' rights that ensures legal certainty within employment relationships.

items.title: IMPLEMENTASI PRINSIP ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND GOVERNANCE (ESG) DAN TANGGUNG JAWAB DIREKSI DALAM KERANGKA GOOD CORPORATE GOVERNANCE: STUDI KASUS PADA PT INTICORP LOGISTICS
items.abstract: Abstract: This study analyses the legal position of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles within the framework of Good Corporate Governance (GCG), examines the implementation of ESG at PT Inticorp Logistics, and assesses the legal responsibility of the Board of Directors for ESG implementation under Indonesian company law. A normative juridical method was used with statutory, conceptual, and normative case study approaches. The analysis drew on Law Number 40 of 2007 on Limited Liability Companies, Financial Services Authority Regulation Number 51/POJK.03/2017, the G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance (2023), the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards, and the doctrines of fiduciary duty, duty of care, duty of loyalty, and the business judgment rule, applied to the company's documents. The findings show that PT Inticorp Logistics has implemented ESG at the operational level through quality management, occupational health and safety systems, and a basic corporate governance structure. However, ESG has not been integrated into the directors' strategic policies, risk management, performance indicators, or sustainability reporting. Indonesian positive law does not explicitly require all companies to adopt ESG, so the absence of an ESG policy does not in itself constitute a breach of law. Nevertheless, ESG holds an implicit legal position as part of the directors' duty to manage the company in good faith and with due care. This study proposes a legal construction of ESG-based directors' responsibility that positions ESG integration as a concrete manifestation of fiduciary duty and duty of care. Keyword: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG); directors' responsibility; fiduciary duty; good corporate governance; logistics company. Penelitian menggunakan metode yuridis normatif dengan pendekatan perundang-undangan, konseptual, dan studi kasus normatif. Analisis didasarkan pada Undang-Undang Nomor 40 Tahun 2007 tentang Perseroan Terbatas, POJK Nomor 51/POJK.03/2017, G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance (2023), IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards, serta doktrin fiduciary duty, duty of care, duty of loyalty, dan business judgment rule yang diterapkan pada dokumen perusahaan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa PT Inticorp Logistics telah menerapkan ESG pada tingkat operasional melalui sistem manajemen mutu, keselamatan dan kesehatan kerja, serta struktur dasar tata kelola perusahaan. items.title: Incorporating natural language processing-derived features from pathology reports into machine learning models to predict differentiated thyroid cancer recurrence
items.abstract: Objective To evaluate the performance of machine learning (ML) models tasked with predicting thyroid cancer recurrence using natural language processing (NLP) and large language model (LLM) derived features. Patients and methods This was a retrospective study of adult thyroid cancer patients treated at an academic medical center between January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2022. Patients were classified as having cancer recurrence or no recurrence. Novel NLP features were extracted from cytopathology and surgical pathology reports using Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), and a zero-shot large language model (LLM) classification. Five learning algorithms (Decision Tree, Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost) were trained to predict cancer recurrence utilizing a combination of NLP-derived features and structured electronic medical record (EMR) variables. All models were evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using F1 score and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). The top performing model was hyperparameter-tuned, and feature importance was evaluated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values and gain-based importance. Results 310 patients with differentiated thyroid cancer diagnosed on final surgical pathology were included in this study. The optimized XGBoost model incorporating EMR variables and LDA-derived features achieved the best performance, with a cross-validated F1 score of 0.647 on the training set and a held-out test F1-score of 0.631 (95% CI 0.509–0.758) and ROC-AUC of 0.741 (95% CI 0.572-0.892). SHAP analysis and gain-based feature importance identified surgical pathology topic—cervical and lateral neck lymph node dissection—as the dominant predictor of cancer recurrence. Conclusion Various classifiers including machine learning models utilizing novel NLP features derived from unstructured pathology reports may enable improved prediction of recurrence in patients with differentiated thyroid cancer.

items.title: Inheritance as an Admission Test for LLM Prompt Merge Operators
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are often improved by iterating until a fixed verifier is done. Once that verifier saturates, the loop has nothing left to climb. We instead score agents against the current population, and a frozen panel records whether anyone got better. The panel mean can rise inside the seeds by elimination alone. We therefore count a run as training only when its final mean beats the best generation-zero member. A merge is admitted only when the child moves toward the donor, past the child the same operator produces at zero dose, and the lower confidence bound on that movement reaches half the requested dose. That is the admission test. A detectable shortfall rejects the operator, and the test is otherwise undetermined. We keep realised fitness ϕas the selector and reference performance θas the unused ruler. Every measurement uses gemini-3.1-flash-lite on one negotiation task, and no fixed-oracle arm was run. In the open loop, tactic append grafts short donor rules and is admitted. Free rewrite moves only a third of the requested dose and is rejected. Template append pastes raw donor replies into the child. Its movement clears the bound on the first probe but not on the re-probe, and it is left undetermined. A held-out re-probe on the five situations the merge never saw confirms that both appends move, and it does not rescue free rewrite. Neither append rises with the dose. Constrained rewrite is admitted in the open loop and was not run in the closed loop, which changes only the operator. The population, the scores and the task stay fixed. No free-rewrite run beats the best generation-zero member. Every tactic-append run and every template-append run does. Sampled loop children keep that split. Free rewrite moves no further toward the donor, and both appends still clear the bound, by less than in the open loop.
